question.text: Endovenous laser ablation in the treatment of small saphenous varicose veins: does site of access influence early outcomes?
question.context: The study was performed to evaluate the clinical and technical efficacy of endovenous laser ablation (EVLA) of small saphenous varicosities, particularly in relation to the site of endovenous access. Totally 59 patients with unilateral saphenopopliteal junction incompetence and small saphenous vein reflux underwent EVLA (810 nm, 14 W diode laser) with ambulatory phlebectomies. Small saphenous vein access was gained at the lowest site of truncal reflux. Patients were divided into 2 groups: access gained above mid-calf (AMC, n = 33) and below mid-calf (BMC, n = 26) levels. Outcomes included Venous Clinical Severity Scores (VCSS), Aberdeen Varicose Vein Questionnaire (AVVQ), patient satisfaction, complications, and recurrence rates. Both groups demonstrated significant improvement in VCSS, AVVQ, generic quality of life Short Form 36, and EuroQol scores (P<.05) up to 1 year. No differences were seen between AMC and BMC groups for complications (phlebitis: 2 [6%] and 1 [3.8%], P>.05; paresthesia: 2 [6%] and 5 [19%], P = .223) and recurrence (3 [9%] and 1 [3.8%], P = .623), respectively.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant difference in complications (phlebitis and paresthesia) or recurrence rates between patients whose access was gained above mid-calf (AMC) and those whose access was gained below mid-calf (BMC). This indicates that the site of access does not influence early outcomes.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: No differences were seen between AMC and BMC groups for complications (phlebitis: 2 [6%] and 1 [3.8%], P>.05; paresthesia: 2 [6%] and 5 [19%], P = .223) and recurrence (3 [9%] and 1 [3.8%], P = .623), respectively.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other factors could influence outcomes, the study specifically focused on the site of access and found no significant difference in complications or recurrence rates, making the site of access the most relevant factor to consider.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no statistically significant differences between the AMC and BMC groups in terms of complications, recurrence rates, or clinical outcomes. Both groups showed significant improvement in VCSS, AVVQ, and quality of life scores, with no differences in phlebitis, paresthesia, or recurrence rates (P >.05, P =.223, P =.623 respectively). This suggests that the site of access does not influence early outcomes in EVLA treatment of small saphenous varicose veins.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: No differences were seen between AMC and BMC groups for complications (phlebitis: 2 [6%] and 1 [3.8%], P>.05; paresthesia: 2 [6%] and 5 [19%], P =.223) and recurrence (3 [9%] and 1 [3.8%], P =.623), respectively.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses were relevant as this is a procedural study evaluating EVLA outcomes. The key consideration was whether access site affects treatment efficacy, which was determined by comparing outcomes between the two groups.

This indicates that site of access does not influence early outcomes.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: No differences were seen between AMC and BMC groups for complications (P>.05) and recurrence (P=.623), with all outcomes showing significant improvement in both groups but no group superiority.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Considered whether access site might affect technical success or complication rates, but the data show no significant differences, ruling out site-dependent efficacy or safety.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: DVT (venous thromboembolism), infection, and deep venous injury were considered but not reported as differing between groups; thus, these specific site-related risks are not supported by the data.
